Two sides agree to try to make bilateral relationship ‘more balanced’ after weeks of threats The EU and China have agreed to enter three months of talks to try to avoid a trade war over the bloc’s €360bn (£310bn) annual import/export imbalance. In their first joint statement in seven years, the two sides agreed in Brussels to open a formal trade consultation after weeks of threats and recriminations from China if the EU imposed any measures to stop the flood of goods and components into the bloc. The EU’s trade commissioner, Maroš Šefčovič, said he hoped the “dialogue would bring tangible results” before the next meeting in Beijing in October. He met his Chinese counterpart, commerce minister Wang Wentao, for talks on Monday as part of a diplomatic offensive.

“We simply cannot afford to continue in the unsustainable growth of the trade deficit from the European perspective,” said Šefčovič. “We just didn’t want to wait too long. You hear it from European leaders, you heard it from the president of the European Commission, that what is very important for us is engagement, it’s dialogue. But it has to bring tangible results, and we believe that we can achieve them by October.” Industry groups including the European Chambers of Commerce in China say the level of exports going to Europe is threatening to “cannibalise” EU factories heavily reliant on components from China. The two sides have agreed to enter into consultation on four areas: the rebalancing of trade and investment; export controls including those on rare earths; intellectual property rights and World Trade Organization reforms.

They said in a joint statement: “The EU and China as key trade partners, agree that the main objective of the TIC [Trade and Investment Consultations] is to strengthen dialogue at ministerial level on trade and investment policies with the view to stabilise and make our bilateral relationship more balanced.” EU leaders met two weeks ago to discuss concerns over what is now widely being described as China Shock 2.0 – a threat to European industries and jobs that extends far beyond electric vehicles and green energy. Eurostat, the EU’s statistics agency, said on 15 June that Chinese exports to the EU outweighed imports from the bloc by €1bn a day.

Two sides agree to try to make bilateral relationship ‘more balanced’ after weeks of threats

The EU and China have agreed to enter three months of talks to try to avoid a trade war over the bloc’s €360bn (£310bn) annual import/export imbalance.

He met his Chinese counterpart, commerce minister Wang Wentao, for talks on Monday as part of a diplomatic offensive.

They said in a joint statement: “The EU and China as key trade partners, agree that the main objective of the TIC [Trade and Investment Consultations] is to strengthen dialogue at ministerial level on trade and investment policies with the view to stabilise and make our bilateral relationship more balanced.”

EU leaders met two weeks ago to discuss concerns over what is now widely being described as China Shock 2.0 – a threat to European industries and jobs that extends far beyond electric vehicles and green energy.

Eurostat, the EU’s statistics agency, said on 15 June that Chinese exports to the EU outweighed imports from the bloc by €1bn a day.

“We simply cannot afford to continue in the unsustainable growth of the trade deficit from the European perspective,” said Šefčovič. “We just didn’t want to wait too long. You hear it from European leaders, you heard it from the president of the European Commission, that what is very important for us is engagement, it’s dialogue. Monday’s meeting (29 June) between Chinese commerce minister Wang Wentao and EU trade commissioner Maroš Šefčovič in Brussels has been billed by EU officials as a make-or-break event for the future of Europe’s trade with the manufacturing superpower.

China’s oversupply and low domestic consumption was “an imbalance that the world just cannot digest,” outgoing EU trade negotiator Sabine Weyand told MEPs in the run up.

Šefčovič’s office had drafted plans for an ‘overcapacity’ instrument that would allow the EU to impose new tariffs on a raft of Chinese industrial goods and import limits.

His officials have also mooted a ‘diversification’ instrument that would force European companies to diversify supply sources in critical sectors, in a move to reduce industrial dependency on China.

But the momentum on putting those measures into law appears to have been lost.

Though a video conference on ‘global economic imbalances’ was held with China ahead of the French-hosted G7 summit last week, officials in Beijing cancelled several meetings with EU counterparts that had been intended to prepare the ground for the Wang-Šefčovič talks.

And at last week’s EU summit in Brussels, national leaders were notably circumspect in their remarks on China.

And all that appears to have kicked the can down the road until the autumn on the new ‘overcapacity’ and ‘diversification’ instruments

France, by contrast, has led calls for stronger tools to contain China's overcapacity and market-distorting subsidies.

payload.title: EU ja Kiina aloittavat kolmen kuukauden kauppaneuvottelut alijäämäkiistan ratkaisemiseksi
payload.summary: EU ja Kiina ovat sopineet kolmen kuukauden neuvotteluista, joilla pyritään tasapainottamaan kauppasuhdetta ja välttämään kauppakiistan kärjistyminen.
payload.content:
EU ja Kiina ovat sopineet kolmen kuukauden kauppaneuvotteluista, joiden tavoitteena on tehdä osapuolten välisestä suhteesta tasapainoisempi ja välttää kauppasodan uhka. Taustalla on EU:n noin 360 miljardin euron vuotuinen tuonti- ja vientiepätasapaino Kiinan kanssa sekä eurooppalainen huoli siitä, että kiinalaisten tavaroiden ja komponenttien virta painaa EU:n teollisuutta.

## Neuvottelut jatkuvat lokakuuhun

Osapuolet sopivat Brysselissä virallisesta kauppa- ja investointikonsultaatiosta. Kyseessä on niiden ensimmäinen yhteinen julkilausuma seitsemään vuoteen. Julkilausuman mukaan EU ja Kiina pitävät toisiaan keskeisinä kauppakumppaneina ja haluavat vahvistaa ministeritason vuoropuhelua kauppa- ja investointipolitiikasta, jotta kahdenvälinen suhde vakautuisi ja tasapainottuisi.

EU:n kauppakomissaari Maroš Šefčovič tapasi maanantaina Kiinan kauppaministerin Wang Wentaon osana diplomaattista valmistelua. Šefčovičin mukaan EU toivoo vuoropuhelulta konkreettisia tuloksia ennen seuraavaa tapaamista, joka on määrä järjestää Pekingissä lokakuussa.

Šefčovič sanoi, ettei EU voi jatkaa tilanteessa, jossa kauppavaje kasvaa eurooppalaisesta näkökulmasta kestämättömällä tavalla. Hänen mukaansa EU:n linjana on sitoutuminen ja vuoropuhelu, mutta sen täytyy johtaa tuloksiin. Hän perusteli aikataulua sillä, ettei EU halunnut odottaa liian pitkään.

## Huoli koskee myös teollisuutta ja työpaikkoja

Neuvotteluissa käsitellään neljää kokonaisuutta: kaupan ja investointien tasapainottamista, vientivalvontaa mukaan lukien harvinaiset maametallit, immateriaalioikeuksia sekä Maailman kauppajärjestön uudistuksia.

Eurooppalaiset teollisuusryhmät, kuten Kiinassa toimivat eurooppalaiset kauppakamarit, ovat varoittaneet, että Eurooppaan suuntautuvan viennin määrä uhkaa heikentää EU:n tehtaita, jotka ovat vahvasti riippuvaisia kiinalaisista komponenteista. Lähdeaineiston mukaan huoli liittyy siihen, että vientivirta voi syödä eurooppalaisten tehtaiden asemaa niiden omilla markkinoilla.

EU-johtajat käsittelivät huolia kaksi viikkoa sitten. Keskusteluissa on kuvattu uutta painetta eurooppalaisille teollisuudenaloille ja työpaikoille, eikä huoli rajoitu vain sähköautoihin tai vihreään energiaan. EU:n tilastovirasto Eurostat kertoi 15. kesäkuuta, että Kiinan vienti EU:hun ylitti EU:n viennin Kiinaan miljardilla eurolla päivässä.

Taustalla on noin 360 miljardin euron vuotuinen kauppavaje EU:n näkökulmasta.

Two sides agree to try to make bilateral relationship ‘more balanced’ after weeks of threats The EU and China have agreed to enter three months of talks to try to avoid a trade war over the bloc’s €360bn (£310bn) annual import/export imbalance. In their first joint statement in seven years, the two sides agreed in Brussels to open a formal trade consultation after weeks of threats and recriminations from China if the EU imposed any measures to stop the flood of goods and components into the bloc. The EU’s trade commissioner, Maroš Šefčovič, said he hoped the “dialogue would bring tangible results” before the next meeting in Beijing in October. He met his Chinese counterpart, commerce minister Wang Wentao, for talks on Monday as part of a diplomatic offensive.

“We simply cannot afford to continue in the unsustainable growth of the trade deficit from the European perspective,” said Šefčovič. “We just didn’t want to wait too long. You hear it from European leaders, you heard it from the president of the European Commission, that what is very important for us is engagement, it’s dialogue. But it has to bring tangible results, and we believe that we can achieve them by October.” Industry groups including the European Chambers of Commerce in China say the level of exports going to Europe is threatening to “cannibalise” EU factories heavily reliant on components from China. The two sides have agreed to enter into consultation on four areas: the rebalancing of trade and investment; export controls including those on rare earths; intellectual property rights and World Trade Organization reforms.

They said in a joint statement: “The EU and China as key trade partners, agree that the main objective of the TIC [Trade and Investment Consultations] is to strengthen dialogue at ministerial level on trade and investment policies with the view to stabilise and make our bilateral relationship more balanced.” EU leaders met two weeks ago to discuss concerns over what is now widely being described as China Shock 2.0 – a threat to European industries and jobs that extends far beyond electric vehicles and green energy. Eurostat, the EU’s statistics agency, said on 15 June that Chinese exports to the EU outweighed imports from the bloc by €1bn a day.
